- Whether the law where she works entitles her to equal pay, which would give her a legal claim against the employer.
- Whether the employer knows about the gap and keeps it on purpose, or it is itself an oversight.
- How much repayment would be demanded, and on what terms.
output.reasoning:
Simone's maxim, if she stays silent, would be: "When I receive money I know was paid to me by mistake, I will keep it quietly, because I judge that I am owed at least that much for a separate wrong done to me." This is close to Kant's own example of a deposit whose owner has no record of it. If everyone kept money they knew had been paid by mistake whenever they felt entitled to it, paying someone would no longer settle what is owed. The practice of paying and receiving under a contract would stop working. So the maxim fails the universality test in the strict sense: it cannot even be thought as a universal law, which marks it as breaking a perfect duty.

The case is harder than a plain theft because Simone is very probably being wronged herself. Paying her $600 less than less experienced men for the same work treats her as a cheaper input rather than as an equal party to the contract, and her grievance is real. But on Kant's theory of right, having a grievance does not make you the judge of your own case. Deciding for herself that part of her claim is settled by keeping an unexplained error is exactly the private self-help that Kant says the civil condition replaces with public procedures. Treating the error as compensation also puts a false account into the relationship, since the employer believes it is paying her contract rate. And the amounts do not even match: the error would cover only half the gap. What she is owed has to be claimed openly, not taken quietly. This is a contemporary application: if equal-pay law gives her a claim, that claim is the proper route, and she has it whether or not she reports the error.

The fear of retaliation is real, but it changes nothing about the error. Staying silent to avoid a bad outcome does not make keeping the money acceptable, and Kant does not let consequences decide what duty requires. The fear does bear on the separate question of the pay gap. Raising it falls under the duty to respect herself and not be servile, and that duty leaves room for judgment about when and how to act. She is not strictly required to raise the gap right now. Handing back what is not hers, however, allows no such room. Kant would not see her honesty as a gift to an employer who has not earned it. It is what she owes as someone who keeps her commitments, whatever the other side has done.
output.strongest_objection: The strongest objection is that the employer has kept back far more than $300 a month from her, so keeping the error only partly corrects an injustice, and Kant cares about rightful possession. My reply is that rightful possession, on his view, has to be settled by public, reciprocal procedures and not by one party deciding alone in her own favour. Her claim to equal pay is valid, but it has to be made openly, through the employer or the law, and not by quietly keeping a mistake.
output.verdict: Yes. Keeping money she knows was paid by mistake breaks a perfect duty of right, and the real wrong of the pay gap does not entitle her to settle it herself. She should report the error, and she is free, and has good reason, to press her equal-pay claim openly as well.
output.would_change_if: If the extra $300 were not an error but a payment the employer knowingly made to her, for example a deliberate or agreed adjustment, it would be rightfully hers and there would be nothing to report.

output.action_rated: Whether Elias should draw his full legal water allocation during the drought, despite the downstream town's request that upstream users voluntarily draw half.
output.established_facts:
- Elias holds a legal right to his full allocation, and the state has declined to order any reduction.
- The downstream town's wells are failing in the third year of drought, and the town has asked upstream users to voluntarily draw half.
- Drawing half would cost Elias about a third of his mature trees, which take a decade to replace. Drawing his full share keeps them alive.
- The town's shortfall would be covered if the four largest upstream users, Elias among them, all drew half.
- If Elias alone draws half, it makes little difference.
output.open_facts:
- Whether the failing wells threaten the town's drinking water and basic needs, or only less essential uses.
- Whether the other three large users would reduce if Elias did, or already intend to.
- Whether losing a third of the trees would ruin Elias financially, or only cost him a serious but bearable loss.
- Whether the town has other sources it could turn to.
output.reasoning:
Start with right. Elias's allocation is a legal right held within a civil order, and the public authority has declined to order a cut. So drawing his full share wrongs no one in the enforceable sense. The town cannot compel him, and he breaks no perfect duty by drawing. If the question were only about duties of right, the answer would be yes.

Duties of virtue are a different matter. Elias's maxim needs to be stated honestly. It is not simply "I will use what is mine." It is closer to: "When others face serious need that I could help meet, I will keep my full entitlement to protect my own property, since my share alone would not solve the problem." Test that as a universal law. It creates no contradiction in conception: a world where everyone reasons this way can be imagined. But it fails the test of what one can will. A rational agent who depends on others in scarcity cannot will a world where each person refuses help because his own part is not enough by itself. And that is exactly the reasoning that would leave the town dry even though the four users together could save it. The "makes little difference" argument does not help Elias. It is the logic that defeats collective duties.

Beneficence is an imperfect duty, and the latitude is real. Elias does not have to sacrifice everything, and he need not give so much that he himself ends up needing charity. A decade-long loss of a third of his trees is a heavy cost, and it counts. But latitude lets one duty limit another, or lets a person choose how to help. It does not allow him to exempt himself because keeping everything is what he would prefer. What he owes depends on facts the case leaves open. If the town faces a threat to drinking water, its claim is urgent, and a serious but survivable loss of trees does not outweigh it. If reducing would ruin Elias, his duty to keep his own means of acting shrinks what he must give.

Treating the townspeople as ends means taking their need as a reason that bears on his choice, not just a request he is free to ignore. A maxim of conditional cooperation can be universalized: draw half, or reduce substantially, commit to it openly, and press the other three to do the same. Drawing the full allocation as the case frames it probably fails what virtue requires, though it violates no one's rights.
output.strongest_objection: The strongest objection is that beneficence is a wide duty. Elias could meet it in other ways, and asking him to sacrifice a decade of his livelihood for an outcome that depends on others he cannot control goes beyond what Kant demands. The reply: that latitude covers how and how much, not whether. The town's need is serious, the remedy is shared and within reach, and the reason for refusing ("my part changes little") cannot be willed as universal law. So Elias still owes a real contribution, even if it is scaled to what he can bear.
output.verdict: No, probably not. Drawing his full share violates no enforceable right, but the maxim behind it fails the universalizability test for beneficence, and his duty of virtue calls for a real reduction coordinated with the other large users.
output.modification: Elias draws half, or reduces as far as he can without ruining himself, commits to this publicly, and actively presses the other three large users to do the same.
output.would_change_if: If reducing would ruin Elias financially, or if the town's need did not concern basic necessities, his duty of beneficence would narrow enough that drawing in full could be permissible.

output.action_rated: Whether the committee should award the full grant to Mei, the applicant with the highest GPA, as the published rule directs.
output.established_facts:
- A published rule at a public college awards one full grant to the applicant with the highest GPA in the cohort.
- Mei has the highest GPA; her parents pay her living costs and she has said she would attend without the grant.
- Dario's GPA is 0.05 lower; he works thirty hours a week and has said he will drop out without the grant.
- The rule gives the committee discretion only where GPAs are tied, and they are not tied.
output.open_facts:
- Whether the college or others have other sources of aid (hardship funds, other scholarships) that could reach Dario.
- Whether the rule was made through legitimate authority for the common good, as opposed to being arbitrary. Nothing suggests it was not.
- Whether Dario's statement that he will drop out is certain or a sincere estimate.
output.reasoning:
The committee members are not private almsgivers spending their own money. They administer common goods under a public rule, so the first question is one of distributive justice: goods held in common should be shared out according to the standard the community has set for them. Here that standard is merit measured by GPA. Nothing about a merit standard is unjust in itself. Rewarding and encouraging learning serves knowledge of truth and the common good. It is not respect of persons, the vice of giving a public good because of a personal feature unrelated to the reason for giving it. In fact, respect of persons is the danger here. To give the grant to Dario because of his need, when the reason the grant exists is academic excellence, would be to distribute it on a ground other than the one it is meant for.

Second, the rule is published. Applicants competed relying on it, and Mei has met its condition. Once the process has run, she has a claim that the committee's own justice must honor. Taking the grant from her would harm her and would also damage trust in public rules. That is a harm to legal justice and to the common good.

Could equity (epieikeia) allow the committee to depart from the rule's wording? Equity applies when following the letter in an unforeseen case would defeat the purpose the lawgiver had in mind. The purpose of a merit grant is to reward the highest achievement. Giving it to Mei fulfills that purpose, so this is not a case where the wording fails its aim. Need was simply never the rule's criterion. A small margin of 0.05 does not change what the standard is. The rule has also already set out its one area of discretion, ties.

Dario's need is real and serious. Charity and mercy toward him are binding on those who can help. That duty falls on the institution and on individuals through other means: hardship funds, advocacy, or asking Mei whether she would be willing to decline or share the award. It cannot be met by taking something owed to someone else. Doing evil so that good may come is not permitted, and the committee cannot give away one person's due to meet another person's need. Separately, the college would do well to consider whether the rule should include a need component in the future. Applying this to a modern scholarship committee is a contemporary use of these principles, not anything Aquinas himself prescribed.
output.strongest_objection: The strongest objection is that in urgent need, material goods become common, and Dario's education is a basic good at stake. The reply: that principle covers extreme necessity where life is at risk, and it does not permit a steward to break a public trust. Dario's need is grave but can be met by other means, so the fitting response is to help him in addition to honoring Mei's claim, not to take the grant from her.
output.verdict: Yes. On this analysis, the grant is owed to Mei under a just public rule that the committee is bound to administer. Dario's need should be met through charity and other channels, not by taking what belongs to her.
output.would_change_if: If Mei freely gave up the grant, or if the rule's own purpose, stated by its authority, included financial need, then awarding it to Dario would become just.

output.action_rated: Whether Nora should tell her dying, lucid father that his estranged son Kevin sent his love, when Kevin in fact refused to send any message.
output.established_facts:
- The father is in his last days, is lucid, and has asked twice whether Kevin has sent word.
- Nora called Kevin yesterday; he said he would not come and would not send a message.
- Kevin cut contact five years ago after a bitter argument.
- The truth will cause the father real grief in the hours he has left.
- The false message would comfort him, and he can never find out it is false.
output.open_facts:
- Whether the father has ever said, while well, that he would rather be spared painful truths at the end of his life.
- Whether Nora could answer truthfully in a gentler form, for example without passing on the harshness of Kevin's refusal, and still satisfy his question.
- Whether the father wants the answer so he can do something with it himself, such as leaving Kevin a message or settling his own affairs.
output.reasoning:
Justice as fairness has no rule for deathbed lies, so this is a contemporary application: it uses the natural duties and Rawls's account of paternalism to answer a private question. It is not something Rawls himself prescribed.

Nora is not filling an institutional role here. What binds her are the natural duties that apply between persons whatever their arrangements: mutual aid, not causing unnecessary suffering, and mutual respect. Mutual respect means treating someone as a moral person, able to form and revise his own view of his life and to judge his own situation.

The pull toward the lie comes from mutual aid, since it would relieve real suffering. But the lie does more than relieve suffering. It swaps a false account of the world for the one the father has asked for. He is lucid and has asked twice. His question is his own attempt to understand how his relationship with his son ended, and that is part of how he sees his own life.

Rawls allows paternalism only in narrow conditions, which the parties in the original position would accept as protection for themselves. It applies when a person's reason is failing or absent. Even then, others should act as that person would choose for himself, guided by his settled preferences. Neither condition holds on the stated facts. The father's reason is intact. Nothing in the case says he would prefer comfort to the truth. His repeated questions point the other way.

Parties who don't know whether they will be the dying parent or the relative at the bedside would not adopt a rule that lets the healthy override a lucid person's direct question whenever they judge that he would be happier deceived. That rule would put everyone's final understanding of his own life at the mercy of other people's judgments of his welfare, and that erodes the social bases of self-respect. The lie also puts words of love in Kevin's mouth that he refused to give, so it misrepresents a third person's considered choice.

If the father had said earlier that he wanted to be spared bad news at the end, that settled preference would change the analysis. Without it, the duty not to harm does not require the lie. It requires compassion in how the truth is told. Nora can say she reached Kevin, that he could not bring himself to send anything, and that she is with her father now. She can also leave out the bitterness of the call.
output.strongest_objection: The lie gives the father only comfort, costs him nothing he will ever notice, and he has so little time left that his capacity to act on the truth hardly matters. Mutual aid seems to weigh most heavily here. In reply: the wrong is not that he might find out. The wrong is that a lucid person's direct question is answered by someone deciding for him what he may believe about his own life. The duty to relieve suffering can be met by telling the truth gently.
output.verdict: She probably should not. Her father is lucid and has asked directly, and inventing Kevin's words would override his own judgment without the conditions that would justify paternalism. Nora should tell him the truth with as much compassion as she can.
output.modification: Nora can answer truthfully but gently: she reached Kevin, he did not send a message, and she is here with her father. She can leave out the harshness of Kevin's refusal and stay with him in his grief.
output.would_change_if: If the father's reason were failing, or he had clearly said earlier that he wanted to be spared painful truths at the end, the comforting message could be justified as acting on his own settled preferences.

output.action_rated: Whether Elias should draw his full legal water allocation from the river for his orchard during the third year of drought, despite the downstream town's request that upstream users voluntarily draw half.
output.established_facts:
- Elias has a legal right to his full allocation, which his family has held for sixty years.
- It is the third year of drought, and the downstream town's wells are failing. The town has asked upstream users to draw half voluntarily. The state has declined to order this.
- If he draws his full share, his mature trees survive. If he draws half, he loses about a third of them, and they take a decade to replace.
- The town's shortfall would be covered if the four largest upstream users, Elias among them, all drew half.
- If Elias alone draws half, it makes little difference to the town.
output.open_facts:
- Whether the other three large users would cut back if Elias did, or if he proposed that all four cut together.
- How severe the town's need is: household and health needs, or lesser uses.
- Whether Elias's household livelihood depends on the orchard so heavily that losing a third of it would ruin them.
- Whether the town has other sources or remedies.
output.reasoning:
Elias's legal right settles what he may do. It does not settle what he should do. The water law was written for ordinary years. A third year of drought, with a neighbouring town's wells failing, is the kind of particular case a general rule did not foresee. Equity corrects the law by asking what a good lawgiver would have allowed if he had been present. It is very hard to believe such a lawgiver meant an upstream orchard's full share to be protected while a town went short. So the fact that the right is legal, and has been held for sixty years, is a weak reason once the purpose behind it is considered. Someone who insists on the exact letter of his rights at his neighbours' expense is what Aristotle calls a stickler for justice to the letter. The equitable person accepts less than the law would give him.

The town and the upstream farms are also partners in one political community. They are bound together by exchange and by a kind of civic friendship. The good citizen does not act only as far as the state compels him. The state's refusal to order cuts leaves the matter to character, and here character shows.

The costs still count. Losing a third of mature trees, which take a decade to replace, is a real harm to Elias's household, and the household is also part of a flourishing life. Generosity is measured against a person's means, and virtue does not require self-ruin. If the orchard is his household's whole livelihood and the loss would ruin it, the mean shifts toward a smaller cut.

The key fact is that his cut alone makes little difference, while cuts by all four large users would solve the problem. A person of practical wisdom would not take this as permission to draw everything. Nor would he make a symbolic sacrifice that costs him a third of his trees and achieves nothing. He would do what the situation actually needs: go to the other three large users and propose that all four draw half, or offer a conditional pledge to cut if they do. As one of the four, he can realistically make this happen. If they agree, he should draw half. If they refuse, a smaller reduction may be reasonable. Even then, his readiness to act shows justice and friendship rather than grasping.

Drawing the full allocation without further thought, as the question puts it, protects his trees and ignores the need of the community he lives in. That leans toward the vice of taking more than one's share, even if it is legal.
output.strongest_objection: Since his cut alone makes little difference, drawing half would cost him a third of his trees for almost nothing. Reason seems to favour keeping his full share. The reply is that this argument only works if Elias stays passive. He is one of just four users whose joint action would solve the problem, so the practically wise response is to bring about that joint action, not to hide behind its absence.
output.verdict: He probably should not simply draw his full allocation. Equity and civic friendship call on him to work with the other three large users so that all four draw half, and to cut back himself on that basis.
output.modification: Elias should propose that the four largest users all draw half, and he should commit to doing so himself, drawing more only if the others refuse and his household would be seriously harmed.
output.would_change_if: If the other three users refused all cooperation and his household depended on the orchard for survival, drawing the full share would become defensible.

output.action_rated: Whether Priya should answer the credit union's direct question truthfully and disclose that she fired Owen for altering a timesheet.
output.established_facts:

- The credit union asked Priya directly whether Owen has ever been disciplined for dishonesty.

- Whether the law or the credit union's rules put a time limit on how far back disqualifying conduct counts, or allow it to be weighed case by case.

Imagine parties who don't know whether they will be depositors, credit union workers, applicants with a blemish, or employers asked for references. They would want institutions that look after other people's money to be able to check honesty reliably, because the least advantaged depositors are the ones who can least afford losses. The whole arrangement only works if references answer honestly when asked. A reference system where people lie out of sympathy gives no information, and it lets down everyone who depends on it. Priya has chosen to give a reference, so she is taking part in a cooperative practice. Lying to a direct, legally required question is free-riding: she would rely on others telling the truth while exempting her own case. Her sympathy for Owen is decent, but she is not entitled to override the institution's judgment with her own private assessment of who has reformed.

The parties behind the veil would also worry about ending up as someone like Owen, marked forever by one small mistake that he admitted. They would want rehabilitation to count, and they would want old or minor offenses to lose weight over time. But the proper place for that protection is the rules themselves: time limits, individual assessment, the right to give context. Individual lies are the wrong tool.
